hook.title: The Isle
hook.content: Isolated for drilling: the nine two-way prepositions, one question, two cases. The set: an (at/on-edge), auf (on-surface), hinter (behind), in (in), neben (beside), über (over), unter (under), vor (in front of), zwischen (between). Ask wo? (where-at — location) → dative. Ask wohin? (where-to — motion) → accusative. Das Bild ist an der Wand (the picture hangs at the wall — dative). Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand (I hang it onto the wall — accusative). The picture never changed — only the question did.

footnotes.title: an vs auf: the German Haunted Pair
footnotes.content: an = vertical attachment (an der Wand — on the wall's face), auf = horizontal surface (auf dem Tisch — on the table top). English 'on' covers both; German splits them. Book on table → auf; painting on wall → an. Memorize the pair as surface vs edge.

pattern.title: The Pair Drill
pattern.content: Drill the pairs side by side: In die Stadt (into the city — motion) / in der Stadt (in the city — location). Auf den Tisch / auf dem Tisch. Unter den Tisch / unter dem Tisch. Vor das Haus / vor dem Haus. Hinter das Haus / hinter dem Haus. Neben den? — neben den Tisch / neben dem Tisch. Zwischen die? — zwischen die Bücher / zwischen den Büchern (zw-! your sibilant family). The motion verbs that trigger accusative: gehen, fahren, kommen, legen, stellen, hängen (hang-onto). The location verbs: sein, liegen, stehen, hängen (be-hanging).
pattern.linguist_note: The motion/location split is the last surviving trace of the Proto-Indo-European accusative of extent-of-motion — Greek and Latin showed it too. German kept the law fully armed; English kept only its verbs (lay/lie).

exercises.prompt: Match each scene with its case-logic:
exercises.target_answer: in die Stadt, in der Stadt, auf den Tisch, auf dem Tisch
exercises.explanation: Same preposition, same nouns — the question (wohin? or wo?) alone decides the case.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich hänge das Bild an _____ Wand.' (I hang the picture onto the wall — motion):
exercises.meaning: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand
exercises.explanation: hängen-onto is motion: wohin? → accusative (die Wand). The hanging picture AT REST would be an der Wand.

exercises.prompt: Which verb is a LOCATION verb (dative trigger)?
exercises.meaning: The location verbs: sein, liegen, stehen, hängen-rest
exercises.explanation: stellen/legen put things somewhere (motion → accusative); stehen/liegen describe what IS somewhere (dative).

exercises.prompt: What English preposition meaning 'in the space separating two things' is the twin of 'zwischen' (from 'zwei' / 'twain')?
exercises.explanation: Both are 'two-one': between = by-twain, zwischen = zwi-schen. The tw→zw twins from topic 5, still counting two.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The picture hangs on the wall' (at rest!)
exercises.target_answer: Das Bild hängt an der Wand
exercises.meaning: Das Bild hängt an der Wand = The picture hangs at the wall

vocab_hints.note: hängen at rest = location → dative: an der Wand. 'Hanging onto' (motion) would take die.

exercises.explanation: hängt (rest) + an + der (dative) — the picture is AT the wall, not going to it. One verb, one case, one calm scene.

summary.outcome: Run wo?/wohin? across all nine two-way prepositions and decline correctly.

use_example.german: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
use_example.english: The picture hangs on the wall.

summary.takeaway: Nine prepositions, one question: wohin? → accusative, wo? → dative — and an/auf split surface from edge.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Wechselpräpositionen Sentence Gym — twenty picture-prompt sentences switching cases.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "Today that is very good"
twist.explanation: Building "Heute ist das sehr gut" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Motion → Accusative, Location → Dative.

in.etymology_derivation: The identical twin of in (Proto-Germanic *in); two-way preposition: motion → accusative, location → dative. [wiktionary]

auf.context_phrase: Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.
auf.context_translation: The book is on the table.
auf.etymology_derivation: The twin of up/on (Proto-Germanic *ufa) — and the separable-prefix particle auf = up. [wiktionary]

über.context_translation: We are speaking about / over the book.

unter.context_phrase: Die Katze ist unter dem Tisch.
unter.context_translation: The cat is under the table.
unter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *undar — the exact twin of under; governs dative (location) and accusative (motion). [wiktionary]

vor.context_phrase: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
vor.context_translation: The car stands in front of the house.
vor.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *furai — the twin of English fore (before, forefather); governs dative and accusative. [wiktionary]

hinter.context_phrase: Das Auto ist hinter dem Haus.
hinter.context_translation: The car is behind the house.
hinter.etymology_derivation: The twin of hind (as in hinder, behind) — *hinterą. Two-way preposition. [wiktionary]

neben.context_phrase: Die Katze schläft neben dem Sofa.
neben.context_translation: The cat sleeps beside the sofa.
neben.etymology_derivation: From the *nahuną 'near' family — kin to English nigh. Two-way preposition. [wiktionary]

zwischen.context_phrase: Der Ball ist zwischen den Büchern.
zwischen.context_translation: The ball is between the books.
zwischen.etymology_derivation: The twin of between (tw → zw + the same -en suffix): 'by-twain' ↔ 'two-ened'. Two-way preposition. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

huhn.context_phrase: Das Huhn legt jeden Tag ein Ei.
huhn.context_translation: The chicken lays an egg every day.
huhn.etymology_derivation: Huhn — from Middle High German huon and Proto-West Germanic *hōn, kin to Dutch hoen and English hen; all from the same Germanic fowl family (PIE *keh₂n-). [wiktionary]

einfach.etymology_derivation: ein 'one' plus the suffix -fach '-fold': literally onefold, the exact comparison Wiktionary itself draws with English onefold. [wiktionary]

fuchs.context_translation: The fox sleeps in the forest.
fuchs.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz, from PIE *púḱsos, the tailed one. English fox is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

unterschreiben.etymology_derivation: A Middle High German calque of Latin subscribere — under-write; unter is the twin of English under, and schreiben is the Latin-loan twin of scribe (English write is the native sibling). [wiktionary]

puppe.context_phrase: Das Kind spielt mit der Puppe.
puppe.context_translation: The child plays with the doll.
puppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin pupa, doll — the same Latin doll-word that gave English puppet through Old French popette. [wiktionary][etymonline]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
